title: Which customer contacts should you prevent, not automate?
summary: Find the causes of recurring support questions, improve information where customers need it, and check outcomes before counting fewer contacts as success.
body_markdown:
Published October 3, 2026 · Updated October 16, 2026


An AI automation plan starts naturally with the work arriving in the support queue: which requests could the AI handle, and how much work would that remove from the team? It is also a chance to examine why customers need to ask for help in the first place. Some demand exists because the service has left them uncertain or unable to complete something that should be straightforward.


Automating the answer can reduce the effort of responding while leaving that problem in place. Clearer delivery expectations, an explanation of a delay or a working password-reset process may spare the customer the need to contact support at all. These are opportunities to improve the experience as well as reduce avoidable work.


The aim is to remove those causes while preserving useful engagement. A customer choosing a product may benefit from advice, and someone with a damaged delivery still needs help. Deciding which demand to prevent and which service to provide gives your automation plan a clearer purpose than reducing the ticket count alone.


## Find the cause behind the ticket category


"Order status" identifies a topic, not the reason for contact. Look at the product, journey stage and information the customer had when they asked.


An eyewear retailer evaluating service improvements told Typewise that customers sometimes did not understand that a specialist lens had to be manufactured externally and would take longer. The team was introducing progress updates and considering a clearer explanation when the order was placed. This was a plan described in a 2026 interview, not a measured reduction in contacts or a Typewise AI result.


Ask the support team to bring recurring questions they can connect to a specific gap. Check the relevant page, form or notification yourself. Include questions answered by phone or first-level teams without a ticket, where you have access to those records; ticket counts alone may miss them.


## Choose a fix the customer will encounter


Put the explanation where the uncertainty begins. A note buried in a help center is unlikely to help someone who needs the information while placing an order.


For a made-to-order item, that might mean a clear delivery expectation beside the purchase decision and updates when its status changes. For a repeated compatibility question, it might mean a product comparison or a compatibility table. These are possible interventions to test, not guaranteed savings.


One of our parcel-logistics customers reported fewer tickets after redesigning delivery notifications with clearer wording and direct options to adjust delivery or give drop-off permission. Other service improvements were happening too, and the source supplied no before-and-after count. It supports investigating the notification design, not attributing a precise reduction to it.


Assign the change to the team that owns the cause: product content, checkout, delivery communications or another part of the service. Automating the explanation can help while that work is pending, but it should not make the upstream problem disappear from the backlog.


## Keep useful advice available


Some questions depend on the customer's situation. A beginner choosing a product or a customer checking an unusual combination may need a conversation even when the documentation is good.


Do not make those contacts harder merely to improve a contact-reduction metric. Decide what can be answered through content, what a conversational system can help clarify and when a person should take over. Verify that the human path is actually staffed.


A simple review can place each recurring question in one of three groups:


Question Likely next step


A customer cannot find a fact you could have shown earlier Improve the page, form or notification and test the change


The answer depends on the customer's needs or judgment Keep an accessible advice path


A legitimate exception remains, such as a damaged delivery Design a clear service workflow with appropriate handover


Treat these as working decisions, not permanent labels. A request may move between groups as the service changes.


## Check outcomes before counting a saving


Measure the specific question before and after the change, alongside the relevant volume of orders or customers. Otherwise a quieter sales period can look like a successful content fix.


Track repeat contacts and other channels where possible. A customer may have stopped using chat and called instead. A customer may also have given up. Fewer messages alone cannot distinguish those outcomes; the[resolution measurement guide](https://www.typewise.app/blog/ai-resolution-metrics-repeat-contacts) explains how to keep unknown outcomes visible.


Choose a useful companion measure: completion of the task, complaints, returns, or whether customers still need help at the same step. Record concurrent changes and avoid claiming causation from a simple before-and-after comparison when other explanations remain.


Start with one recurring question and the page or process that appears to cause it. Make a specific change, watch that question and its customer outcome, then decide what demand remains worth[automating](https://www.typewise.app/blog/which-customer-service-tickets-automate-first) .
